extraction.name: Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge
extraction.description: We present a new question set, text corpus, and baselines assembled to encourage AI research in advanced question answering. Together, these constitute the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC), which requires far more powerful knowledge and reasoning than previous challenges such as SQuAD or SNLI. The ARC question set is partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set, where the Challenge Set contains only questions answered incorrectly by both a retrieval-based algorithm and a word co-occurence algorithm. The dataset contains only natural, grade-school science questions (authored for human tests), and is the largest public-domain set of this kind (7,787 questions).
extraction.creator: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord
extraction.citeAs: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord. Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. arXiv preprint arXiv:1803.05457, 2018.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The ARC Dataset consists of a collection of 7787 natural science questions, namely questions authored for use on standardized tests. For ARC we have addressed this through several months of extensive search and investigation. The ARC Corpus was created by utilizing a major search engine to run a large series of search queries relevant to science. Queries were automatically constructed by instantiating 100 hand-written templates for 80 science topics covered by US elementary and middle schools. The top several documents from each search were collected and de-duplicated, and then the content of these documents was stripped down to capture just the text in each document. The resulting text was then chunked into sentences. The corpus was then augmented with the AristoMini corpus, an earlier corpus containing dictionary definitions from Wiktionary, articles from Simple Wikipedia tagged as science, and additional science sentences collected from the Web.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Web Scraping, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The ARC Dataset consists of 7787 natural science questions authored for use on standardized tests. The ARC Corpus contains 14M science-related sentences mined from the Web, collected by running search queries constructed from hand-written templates and science terms. It was augmented with the AristoMini corpus (dictionary definitions from Wiktionary, Simple Wikipedia science articles, and additional science sentences from the Web).
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The ARC question set is partitioned into a Challenge Set (2590 questions) and an Easy Set (5197 questions). The Challenge Set contains questions answered incorrectly by both a retrieval-based algorithm and a word co-occurrence algorithm, while the Easy Set contains the remainder.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the ARC Corpus, collected documents were de-duplicated, their content stripped down to capture just text, and then chunked into sentences. For the questions, during conversion to assertions for entailment models, phrases common in multiple-choice questions (e.g., 'of the following', 'of these') were dropped.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The ARC dataset contains natural, grade-school science questions authored for human tests by examiners.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is assembled to encourage AI research in advanced question answering, addressing limitations of previous datasets that focused on retrieval-style tasks. Progress on ARC would be a significant step forward for the community in developing more advanced QA methods requiring reasoning and deeper text comprehension.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Encourage AI research in advanced question answering. The dataset is partitioned into train/dev/test sets for training, testing, and validation of QA models. The ARC Corpus is provided as an optional resource for systems, which are not restricted to its use.
